name: Chocolate Chunk Cookies
headnote: Joanne Chang builds her chocolate chunk cookie around chocolate hand-chopped off bricks rather than chips, so the pieces are large and irregular and the chocolate flavor is more pronounced. She blends bittersweet with a little milk chocolate for a rounder flavor, and cuts bread flour into the all-purpose for extra structure and chew. The method is fussy on purpose: eggs cracked separately and added one at a time, long creaming to aerate the butter and sugar, and a multi-hour chill before baking, all of which give a lighter, crisper cookie.
flags: Author and recipe name match the collection's source (Flour / Joanne Chang) exactly; this is Chang's own published version of the Flour bakery cookie, hosted on MasterClass rather than the cookbook itself.

name: Corn Bread
headnote: This is the cornbread served at Durgin-Park, the long-running Boston market-district restaurant, taken from The Durgin-Park Cookbook. The defining instruction is to mix the batter by hand and stop as soon as it comes together. Machine mixing develops the batter too far and turns the result cakey instead of the dense, grainy, moist square the restaurant is known for.
comment_digest: The single reviewer confirmed the result is dense and moist and stressed that the hand-mixing instruction is the step that matters; using a mixer produces a cake-like texture instead.
flags: Recipe name and source (Durgin Park) both match the collection record; page credits The Durgin-Park Cookbook.

name: Currant Scones
headnote: Nicole at Baking Bites reprints the currant scone from The Cheese Board: Collective Works, the cookbook of the Berkeley bakery collective, where it was the original bestseller at several hundred a day on a busy Saturday. Her framing is that a scone this rich in butter and cream is worth eating occasionally rather than apologizing for. The high fat and the pairing of heavy cream with buttermilk are what keep the crumb moist and tender while the outside stays slightly crisp.
comment_digest: One reader found the dough far too wet to handle as written. Another asked about adjusting for a convection oven, having had them come out dry. No consensus correction offered by the author.
flags: Page explicitly credits The Cheese Board: Collective Works, matching the collection's recorded source.

name: Farfalle With Salmon
headnote: Giuliano Hazan notes that salmon is not a traditional Italian pasta fish, but that its richness takes well to the standard Italian treatment. He builds the sauce the way an Italian cook would if salmon were common there: a fresh tomato base started with garlic and olive oil, with the fish added late so it stays moist. The approach keeps the salmon from drying out while the tomato and chile carry the seasoning.
flags: Correct author (Giuliano Hazan) and a near-identical title, but the page is on ckbk and mostly paywalled, so only a partial ingredient list was visible. It is from Thirty Minute Pasta; the family version may instead come from The Classic Pasta Cookbook. Same author either way.

name: Cocoa Chocolate Cake
headnote: This is Hershey's own back-of-the-can cocoa cake, written for beginners: everything is pantry staples and the batter is stirred together rather than built in stages. The cocoa carries all the chocolate flavor, so no melted chocolate or special technique is needed. The distinguishing step is a cup of boiling water stirred into the finished batter, which blooms the cocoa and leaves the batter very thin, producing an unusually moist, tender crumb.
flags: The collection records the source as the MacArthurs' Hershey's cocoa can, and this is Hershey's current official can/box recipe. Hershey has printed several different cake recipes on its cocoa containers over the decades (e.g. the older Deep Dark Chocolate Cake), so the family's card may be from an earlier can. Same brand and same genre; exact vintage unverified.

name: Cookie Jar Ginger Snaps
headnote: Contributed by Deb Handy of Kansas, this is the soft-and-chewy style of gingersnap rather than the brittle kind. Shortening creamed with sugar gives lift without spreading too much, and molasses supplies both the flavor and the tenderness that keeps the centers soft. The recipe hinges on measuring the flour accurately and pulling the cookies before they look done, since overbaking turns them hard.
flags: The collection card has no recorded source. The name is distinctive and matches Taste of Home's recipe exactly by URL slug, but the page now displays under the retitled heading 'Gingersnap Cookies', so the title match is by slug and history rather than on-page text. Cannot prove the family card came from Taste of Home.

name: Crockpot Rosemary Pork and Mushrooms with Shallots
rating: 5 reviews; star value not numerically shown
headnote: Posted by BeckyF as a family recipe that reminds her of her mother's cooking. Sliced pork shoulder goes into the slow cooker with shallots, mushrooms, rosemary and canned tomatoes and cooks unattended. The long, low heat is what makes it work: it renders the connective tissue in the shoulder so the slices turn tender, while the rosemary and tomato have time to melt into a sauce.
comment_digest: Several cooks increased the rosemary well past the listed tablespoon, saying the dish reads bland at the written seasoning level. One substituted a bay leaf plus Worcestershire when out of rosemary. Doubling the mushrooms is a common tweak, and the usual serving suggestion is over rice or egg noodles.
flags: Recipe title matches the card almost word for word and the source recorded is Crock-Pot; the ingredient list matches the dish name exactly.

name: Cranberry Feta Pinwheels
rating: 24 reviews; star value not numerically shown
headnote: Joy Manning's no-bake party appetizer: whipped cream cheese loosened and blended with crumbled feta, green onion and dried cranberries, spread on large flour tortillas, rolled and sliced. It works on contrast rather than cooking, plush cream cheese against salty feta and chewy sweet cranberry. Rolling the logs and chilling them before slicing both firms the filling and lets the flavors settle, so it is deliberately a make-ahead.
flags: Exact title match and this is the most widely circulated original of the dish, but the collection records the source as 'Susan Symmes - Christmas '22', i.e. passed along within the family. Cannot prove Susan's card came from Taste of Home rather than one of the many blog clones.
